p.src: Now the First Emperor raised an army for an eastern campaign. Zhao Yun remonstrated: “The enemy of the realm is Cao Cao, not Sun Quan. Now Cao Pi has usurped the Han, provoking the wrath of gods and men alike. Your Majesty should swiftly plan a campaign into Guanzhong and station troops on the upper Wei River to punish the wicked usurper; then the loyal men east of the passes will surely shoulder provisions, spur their horses, and welcome the royal army. But if you leave Wei untouched and attack Wu, once the armies clash, how can the conflict quickly be ended? I beg Your Majesty to consider this.” The First Emperor said, “Sun Quan murdered my brother. Moreover, Fu Shiren, Mi Fang, Pan Zhang, and Ma Zhong are all my bitter enemies. Only when I have devoured their flesh and exterminated their clans will my hatred be appeased. Why do you hinder me?” Zhao Yun said, “The feud with the enemy of Han is a public matter. The feud over a brother is a private matter. I beg you to place the realm above all else.” The First Emperor replied, “If I do not avenge my brother, what value are ten thousand leagues of rivers and mountains?” Thus he rejected Zhao Yun’s counsel and issued orders to raise an army against Wu. He also sent an envoy to Wuxi to borrow fifty thousand tribal troops, who were to coordinate with his forces. At the same time, he dispatched an envoy to Langzhong, promoting Zhang Fei to General of Chariots and Cavalry, while retaining his offices as Colonel Director of Retainers, Marquis of Xixiang, and governor of Langzhong. The envoy departed carrying the imperial edict.

p.src: Now Zhang Fei was in Langzhong. When he learned that Lord Guan had been killed by Eastern Wu, he wailed day and night until blood soaked the front of his robe. His officers tried to console him with wine, but the more he drank, the fiercer his rage became. Above and below his command, anyone who offended him was immediately flogged. Many were flogged to death. Each day he faced south, grinding his teeth and glaring in fury and hatred, and never ceased his anguished wailing. Suddenly he was told that an envoy had arrived. He hurriedly admitted him and opened and read the imperial decree. Having accepted his new rank, Zhang Fei bowed toward the north, then laid out wine to entertain the envoy. Zhang Fei said, “My brother was murdered, and my enmity is as deep as the sea. Why have the ministers at court not urged that an army be raised at once?” The envoy replied, “Many have advised destroying Wei first and attacking Wu afterward.” Zhang Fei angrily cried, “What sort of talk is that! Long ago, we three swore brotherhood in the Peach Garden and vowed to share life and death. Now, by cruel fortune, my second brother has died before his time. How could I alone enjoy wealth and honor? I shall seek an audience with the Son of Heaven and ask to serve as vanguard, wearing mourning as I attack Wu, capture the traitors alive, and offer them before my second brother’s spirit, thereby fulfilling our former oath!” With that, he accompanied the imperial envoy toward Chengdu.

p.src: Meanwhile, the First Emperor personally drilled his troops each day on the parade ground, fixing a date to mobilize and lead the campaign in person. The dukes and ministers therefore gathered at the chancellor’s residence and said to Kongming, “The Son of Heaven has only just ascended the throne. For him to command the army in person is no way to safeguard the state. As chancellor, you hold the scales of government. Why do you not remonstrate with him?” Kongming replied, “I have earnestly remonstrated several times, but he simply will not listen. Today, gentlemen, follow me to the parade ground and let us remonstrate again.” Kongming then led all the officials before the First Emperor and memorialized: “Your Majesty has only just ascended the precious throne. If you intend to campaign north against the enemies of Han and proclaim righteousness throughout the realm, then it would be fitting to command the imperial armies in person. But if you merely intend to attack Wu, it is enough to appoint a great general to lead the army. Why trouble Your Sacred Person to go?” Seeing Kongming remonstrate so earnestly, the First Emperor’s resolve softened somewhat. Suddenly word came that Zhang Fei had arrived, and the First Emperor hastily summoned him. Zhang Fei entered the martial hall, prostrated himself, clasped the First Emperor’s feet, and wept. The First Emperor wept as well. Zhang Fei said, “Now that Your Majesty has become sovereign, you have already forgotten our oath in the Peach Garden! Why do you not avenge my second brother?” The First Emperor replied, “Many officials have remonstrated and opposed it, so I have not dared act rashly.” Zhang Fei said, “How could others understand the oath we swore long ago? If Your Majesty will not go, I shall sacrifice this body to avenge my second brother! If I cannot avenge him, I would rather die than see Your Majesty again!” The First Emperor said, “I shall go with you. Lead your own troops out from Langzhou. I shall lead the picked troops and rendezvous with you at Jiangzhou. Together we shall attack Eastern Wu and wipe away this hatred.” As Zhang Fei was about to depart, the First Emperor warned him: “I have long known that when drunk you fly into violent rages, flog your stout soldiers, and then keep the victims beside you. This is the way to invite disaster. From now on, you must be forbearing and never behave as before.” Zhang Fei bowed in farewell and departed.

p.src: Now Zhang Fei returned to Langzhong and issued an order throughout the army: white banners and white armor were to be prepared within three days, so that all three divisions might wear mourning on the campaign against Wu. The next day, two junior officers under his command, Fan Qiang and Zhang Da, entered his tent and reported, “White banners and armor cannot be procured at such short notice. We must be granted more time.” Zhang Fei flew into a rage: “I burn to avenge my brother and bitterly regret that I cannot reach the traitors’ territory tomorrow. How dare you disobey my military order!” He ordered the guards to bind them to trees and give each man fifty lashes across the back. When the flogging was done, he pointed at them and said, “Everything must be ready tomorrow! If you miss the deadline, I shall execute you both before the whole army!” Beaten until their mouths were full of blood, the two returned to their camp and conferred. Fan Qiang said, “We were punished today. How can we possibly have everything ready tomorrow? His temper is as violent as fire. If it is not finished tomorrow, we shall both be killed!” Zhang Da said, “If he is going to kill us, we would do better to kill him first.” Fan Qiang said, “But how can we get near him?” Zhang Da said, “If we are not fated to die, he will be lying drunk upon his bed. If we are fated to die, he will not be drunk.” The two settled their plan.

p.src: Now Zhang Fei sat in his tent, his mind in turmoil and his every movement distracted. He asked his officers, “My heart now pounds and my flesh trembles; whether sitting or lying, I find no peace. What can this mean?” An officer replied, “My lord, this is because you are grieving for Lord Guan.” Zhang Fei ordered wine brought and drank with his officers. Before he knew it, he was thoroughly drunk and lay down in his tent. The two villains, Fan and Zhang, learned of this. At the first watch, each concealed a short knife and secretly entered the tent, pretending that they had an urgent confidential matter to report, and went straight to the bedside. It happened that Zhang Fei never closed his eyes when he slept. That night, as he slept in the tent, the two villains saw his beard bristling and his eyes wide open, and at first dared not strike. Only when they heard his breathing thunder like a peal did they dare approach and plunge their short knives into his belly. Zhang Fei gave one great cry and died. He was fifty-five years old. p.src: That very night, the two villains cut off Zhang Fei's head and fled with several dozen men to Eastern Wu. The next day, when the army learned of it, troops were sent in pursuit, but they could not overtake them. Wu Ban immediately drafted a memorial and reported the matter to the emperor; then he had Zhang Fei's eldest son, Zhang Bao, prepare an inner and outer coffin in which to place the body, ordered the younger son, Zhang Shao, to guard Langzhong, and sent Bao himself to report to the First Sovereign, who had already chosen the date for the campaign. p.src: That night, however, the First Sovereign was seized by alarm and trembling and could not rest in his bed. He went outside his tent and looked up at the heavens. In the northwest he saw a star as large as a dipper suddenly fall to earth. Greatly troubled, the First Sovereign sent someone that very night to ask Kongming about it. Kongming replied in a memorial, “It signifies the loss of a great general. Within three days, an urgent report will surely arrive.” Because of this, the First Sovereign held his troops and made no move. Suddenly, an attendant reported, “Wu Ban, an officer under General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhang at Langzhong, has sent a messenger bearing a memorial.” The First Sovereign stamped his foot and cried, “Alas! My third brother is lost!” When he read the memorial, it indeed bore the grievous news of Zhang Fei's death. The First Sovereign wailed aloud and fell senseless to the ground. The officials revived him. The following day, word came that a body of troops was approaching as swiftly as a gale. The First Sovereign went out of camp to see them. After a long while, a young officer appeared, clad in a white robe and silver armor. He tumbled from his saddle, prostrated himself, and wept. It was Zhang Bao. Bao said, “Fan Qiang and Zhang Da murdered my father and fled to Eastern Wu with his head!” The First Sovereign's grief was so great that he would take neither food nor drink. The ministers earnestly remonstrated: “Your Majesty is just about to avenge your two brothers. How can you first ruin your own imperial health?” Only then did the First Sovereign take some food; then he said to Zhang Bao, “Will you and Wu Ban dare lead your own troops as the vanguard and avenge your father?” Bao replied, “For my country and my father, I would not shrink from ten thousand deaths!” Just as the First Sovereign was about to order Bao to mobilize, another strong contingent swept in like the wind. The First Sovereign ordered an attendant to investigate. Presently, the attendant led into the camp a young general in a white robe and silver armor, who prostrated himself and wept. The First Sovereign looked and saw that it was Guan Xing. At the sight of Guan Xing, the First Sovereign thought of Lord Guan and again burst into loud weeping. The officials entreated him again and again. The First Sovereign said, “I remember when I was still a commoner, Guan, Zhang, and I swore brotherhood and vowed to share life and death. Now that I have become emperor, I wished to share rank and riches with my two brothers, but tragically both have died unnatural deaths! How can the sight of these two nephews fail to break my heart?”

p.src: Traveling through the night, Chen Zhen reached Qingcheng. He had a villager guide him deep into the mountain valley, where he saw the immortal's dwelling in the distance, half veiled by pure clouds and surrounded by an extraordinary auspicious radiance. Suddenly, a young boy came to meet him and said, “Can the visitor be none other than Chen Xiaoqi?” Chen Zhen was greatly astonished. “How does the immortal youth know my name?” he asked. The boy replied, “Last night my master said, ‘An imperial summons is certain to arrive today; and the envoy is certain to be Chen Xiaoqi.’” Chen Zhen said, “He truly is an immortal! What people say is indeed no falsehood!” He then entered the immortal's dwelling with the boy, paid his respects to Li Yi, and proclaimed the emperor's summons. Li Yi pleaded old age and refused to go. Chen Zhen said, “The emperor urgently desires to see you just once, venerable immortal. I beg you not to withhold your crane-borne presence.” Only after repeated and earnest entreaties did Li Yi consent. When he reached the imperial camp, he entered and was received by the First Sovereign. The First Sovereign saw that Li Yi had crane-white hair and a youthful face, blue eyes with square pupils that shone brilliantly, and a body like an ancient cypress. Knowing him to be an extraordinary man, he treated him with exceptional courtesy. Li Yi said, “I am merely a rustic old man from the barren mountains, without learning or knowledge. Your Majesty has honored me with a summons, but I do not know what instruction you have for me.” The First Sovereign said, “For more than thirty years, my two brothers Guan and Zhang and I have been bound by a covenant of life and death. Now both my brothers have been murdered, and I am personally leading a great army to avenge them, but I do not know whether good or ill will come of it. I have long heard that you understand the mysteries of fate, venerable immortal, and beg you to instruct me.” Li Yi replied, “This belongs to Heaven's ordinance and is not something this old man can know.” The First Sovereign questioned him again and again. At last, Li Yi asked for paper and brush and drew more than forty pictures of soldiers, horses, weapons, and armor. When he had finished, he tore every one of them to pieces. He then drew a great man lying face upward on the ground, with another man beside him digging earth to bury him, and wrote a large character, “white,” above them. He then bowed his head to the ground and departed. The First Sovereign was displeased and said to his ministers, “That old man is a madman! He is not to be believed!” He immediately had the drawings burned and urged the army onward.

u.src: Traveling through the night, Chen Zhen reached Qingcheng. He had a villager guide him deep into the mountain valley, where he saw the immortal's dwelling in the distance, half veiled by pure clouds and surrounded by an extraordinary auspicious radiance.
Suddenly, a young boy came to meet him and said, “Can the visitor be none other than Chen Xiaoqi?”
Chen Zhen was greatly astonished. “How does the immortal youth know my name?” he asked.
The boy replied, “Last night my master said, ‘An imperial summons is certain to arrive today;
and the envoy is certain to be Chen Xiaoqi.’”
Chen Zhen said, “He truly is an immortal!
What people say is indeed no falsehood!”
He then entered the immortal's dwelling with the boy, paid his respects to Li Yi, and proclaimed the emperor's summons.
Li Yi pleaded old age and refused to go.
Chen Zhen said, “The emperor urgently desires to see you just once, venerable immortal. I beg you not to withhold your crane-borne presence.”
Only after repeated and earnest entreaties did Li Yi consent. When he reached the imperial camp, he entered and was received by the First Sovereign.

The First Sovereign saw that Li Yi had crane-white hair and a youthful face, blue eyes with square pupils that shone brilliantly, and a body like an ancient cypress. Knowing him to be an extraordinary man, he treated him with exceptional courtesy.
Li Yi said, “I am merely a rustic old man from the barren mountains, without learning or knowledge.
Your Majesty has honored me with a summons, but I do not know what instruction you have for me.”
The First Sovereign said, “For more than thirty years, my two brothers Guan and Zhang and I have been bound by a covenant of life and death.
Now both my brothers have been murdered, and I am personally leading a great army to avenge them, but I do not know whether good or ill will come of it.
I have long heard that you understand the mysteries of fate, venerable immortal, and beg you to instruct me.”
Li Yi replied, “This belongs to Heaven's ordinance and is not something this old man can know.”

The First Sovereign questioned him again and again. At last, Li Yi asked for paper and brush and drew more than forty pictures of soldiers, horses, weapons, and armor. When he had finished, he tore every one of them to pieces.

He then drew a great man lying face upward on the ground, with another man beside him digging earth to bury him, and wrote a large character, “white,” above them. He then bowed his head to the ground and departed.
The First Sovereign was displeased and said to his ministers, “That old man is a madman!
He is not to be believed!”
He immediately had the drawings burned and urged the army onward.

p.src: Zhang Bao entered and reported, “Wu Ban's troops have arrived. I beg to serve as the vanguard.” Admiring his spirit, the First Sovereign immediately took the seal of the vanguard commander and bestowed it upon Zhang Bao. Just as Bao was about to hang the seal at his waist, another young officer strode forward indignantly and cried, “Leave that seal for me!” They looked and saw that it was Guan Xing. Bao said, “I have already received the imperial command.” Guan Xing said, “What ability do you possess that you dare assume this charge?” Bao replied, “I have practiced the martial arts since childhood, and none of my arrows ever misses.” The First Sovereign said, “I should like to see the martial skill of my worthy nephews and determine which of you is superior.” Bao ordered the soldiers to set up a flag a hundred paces away, with a red bull's-eye painted on it. Bao took up his bow and arrows and loosed three shafts in succession; all three struck the red center. Everyone acclaimed his skill. Guan Xing took his bow in hand and said, “What is remarkable about striking a red bull's-eye?” As he spoke, a line of wild geese happened to pass overhead. Guan Xing pointed and said, “I shall shoot down the third of those flying geese.” He loosed a single arrow, and that goose fell at the twang of the bowstring. Civil and military officials alike cheered in unison. Enraged, Bao sprang onto his horse, leveled the eighteen-foot tempered-steel spear his father had wielded, and shouted, “Do you dare match your martial skill against mine?” Guan Xing also mounted, snatched up the great saber handed down in his family, and spurred forth, saying, “Are you the only one who can wield a spear? Do you think I cannot wield a saber?”

p.src: Just as the two young commanders were about to cross weapons, the First Emperor shouted, “You two, cease this insolence!” Guan Xing and Zhang Bao hurriedly dismounted, each casting aside his weapon, and prostrated themselves to beg forgiveness. The First Emperor said, “Ever since I formed a bond of sworn brotherhood at Zhuo Commandery with your fathers, we have been as close as flesh and bone. Now you two likewise stand as brothers and ought to unite your hearts and strength to avenge your fathers together. How can you quarrel and contend with each other, forsaking the greater duty? If you behave so while your fathers’ deaths are still recent, what will become of you in days to come?” The two bowed again and acknowledged their fault. The First Emperor asked, “Which of you two is the elder?” Zhang Bao replied, “I am one year older than Guan Xing.” The First Emperor at once ordered Guan Xing to acknowledge Zhang Bao as his elder brother. Before the command tent, the two broke an arrow in token of their oath and vowed to protect and aid each other forever. The First Emperor issued an edict appointing Wu Ban as vanguard and commanding Zhang Bao and Guan Xing to guard the imperial person. The forces advanced by land and water together, ships and cavalry moving side by side. In a vast and mighty host, they swept toward the realm of Wu.

p.src: Meanwhile, Fan Qiang and Zhang Da took Zhang Fei’s severed head and offered it to the Marquis of Wu, giving him a detailed account of all that had happened. After hearing them out, Sun Quan took the two men into his service and said to his officials, “Liu Xuande has now assumed the imperial throne and commands more than seven hundred thousand elite troops. He is leading the expedition in person, and his might is formidable. What are we to do?” All the officials turned pale and stared at one another. Zhuge Jin stepped forward and said, “I have long enjoyed my lord’s bounty, yet have rendered no service worthy of it. I am willing to risk what remains of my life and go before the ruler of Shu, explain where advantage and peril lie, and bring our two states to peace so that together we may punish Cao Pi for his crimes.” Sun Quan was overjoyed and immediately sent Zhuge Jin as his envoy to persuade the First Emperor to withdraw his army.
